# Can I Drive My 4WD 4Runner on Front Wheels Only?

If you are stuck with a Toyota 4Runner suffering from a seized differential and extensive frame corrosion, your instinct to isolate the working drivetrain is logical. You essentially want to convert your permanent four-wheel-drive vehicle into a temporary front-wheel-drive setup. The short answer is yes, you can operate the vehicle using only the front wheels without replacing the rear end entirely. However, doing so requires understanding how the transfer case and differentials interact mechanically on older 4Runners.

In a standard 4WD configuration like the one found in your 1997 model, the transfer case acts as the central distribution hub. It sends torque to both front and rear axles. If you engage 4WD High or Low with a locked or seized rear differential, you create immediate mechanical conflict. The transfer case attempts to rotate the output shafts at equal speeds (in high range) or specific ratios (in low range). Because your rear diff is locked due to lack of oil and internal seizure, it will not allow the left and right wheels on that axle to rotate independently. This creates a binding situation where the front wheels fight against the solid, non-rotating rear differential.

To run the vehicle safely as a front-wheel-drive unit, you must physically disconnect the power path from the transfer case to the rear axles. Based on your description of the frame and major members being rotted out, this is likely where the labor-intensive work lies. You do not necessarily need to swap the entire rear differential housing if the carrier can be isolated, but you will almost certainly have to remove the driveshaft.

The procedure generally involves removing the rear driveshaft at both ends. At the transfer case end, you will remove the bolts securing the U-joint or flange connection. At the axle end, you must unbolt the differential yokes from the axles themselves. Since your rear diff is seized and the surrounding frame members are compromised, you might find that the carrier assembly needs to be pulled out of the frame rails entirely. This allows you to remove the driveshaft without trying to torque a bolt into a rusted-out bracket or damaging the transfer case output shaft.

Once the driveline connection is severed at the rear, the transfer case will no longer send power back there when engaged in 4WD. However, there is a critical safety consideration regarding the transfer case selection mechanism. If you leave the transfer case lever in 2H (Two-Wheel High) or 4H/4L, the internal gears are engaged to drive the rear output shafts. While these shafts won't move power if disconnected, leaving them under tension while driving on pavement can stress components and potentially cause noise or vibration as the front driveshaft spins without a load on the opposite side of the case.

The safest operational method is to disconnect the rear driveline, ensure the rear wheels are free-spinning (perhaps by removing the axle shafts if the carrier remains in place), and then engage 2H. This isolates the transfer case so it only powers the front axle. If you must drive with the lever in 4WD High because your dashboard switch is broken or you need to lock the center differential for other reasons, ensure the rear axles are completely decoupled from the carrier before attempting to move the vehicle.

If the labor required to remove the driveshaft and disconnect the rear carrier exceeds the cost of a new rear end installation, it may be more economical to simply leave the transfer case in 2H permanently. This effectively renders the vehicle front-wheel-drive without needing to perform any invasive surgery on the rusty frame rails. Just remember that you lose the ability to lock the center differential or utilize 4WD capabilities until the structural integrity of the rear end is restored.
